intro: One global quantization scale can waste resolution on smaller channels. Explore a separate symmetric INT8 scale for each row of a linear layer.
task: Quantize the supplied weight rows, reconstruct them, and calculate a linear output. Return the stored integers and scales so the approximation is inspectable.
requirements: Nonzero weights must have magnitude at least 1e-300 so their per-channel scales remain representable in float64.
x is a nonempty array with shape (..., in_features), weight is a nonempty (out_features, in_features) matrix, and bias has shape (out_features,).
For each weight row, scale = max(abs(row))/127. Use scale=1 for an all-zero row. Round weight/scale to nearest integer with ties to even, clip to [-127,127], then cast to np.int8.
Return a dictionary with weight_int8 (np.int8 matrix), scale (float array of shape (out_features,1)), and output = x @ (weight_int8.astype(float)*scale).T + bias.
Inputs must be real numeric values with finite magnitude at most 1e30. Leave inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Keep one scale per output
hints.body: Reduce the absolute weights over input features and retain the singleton axis.

hints.title: Define zero behavior
hints.body: An all-zero row cannot use zero as a divisor. Its stored integers stay zero when you choose scale one.

explanation: The largest magnitude in each nonzero row maps to 127. Smaller weights share that row scale, so reconstruction introduces bounded rounding error.

The exercise uses a symmetric [-127,127] range and ties-to-even rounding. The upstream class clips to [-128,127] and adds a tiny denominator epsilon; this adaptation makes the zero-row behavior explicit instead.

Only weight storage is INT8 here. The forward pass reconstructs floating weights and performs a floating matmul. It is not an integer kernel or a demonstration of a fourfold total-model memory reduction.
